sentences.text: The genus Palaelodus was first described by Alphonse Milne-Edwards in 1863.
Its name combines Ancient Greek words meaning 'ancient' and 'inhabitant of marshes'.
Palaelodus ambiguus stands as one of the best-known species within this group.
The skull features unique nasal gland depressions located between the eye sockets, a trait not seen in any other known bird.
These birds possessed straight, conical beaks that were not adapted for filter feeding.
The temporal fossae show an intermediate condition between grebes and flamingos, being more pronounced than in flamingos but not as deep as in grebes.
Palaelodus haroldocontii is considered a large species, larger than P. pledgei, P. gracilipes, and P. crassipes.
Palaelodus aotearoa was a medium-sized bird substantially larger than the contemporary Australian species P. pledgei.
Salt glands indicate that these birds foraged in saline or brackish waters.
Juvenile specimens found at Australian lake deposits show that Palaelodus bred and nested in these localities.
Milne-Edwards described the genus based on fossils from the Saint-Gérand-le-Puy area in France.
Largely complete crania of Palaelodus were not described until 1992 by Cheneval and Escuillié.
Palaelodus kurochkini was described from Miocene remains found in Mongolia.
Remains were first recognized in Australia in 1982 but were not formally described until 1998.
Mayr argues that traits like compressed toes and reduced toe flexibility support a swimming lifestyle, suggesting the webbed feet acted as stiff paddles.
Recent research suggests Palaelodus may have used stiff toes as paddles to swim while feeding on insect larvae and snails.
Enlarged fossae on the mandible suggest Palaelodus used head movement for foraging in a way different from flamingos.
Palaelodus likely assumed a different feeding position than flamingos because its spine lacked a pronounced kink.
Milne-Edwards proposed that the diet included larvae of caddisflies and snails found at Saint-Gérand-le-Puy.
It is possible Palaelodids specialized in feeding on small invertebrates, setting the groundwork for later flamingo filter feeding.
Worthy and colleagues argue that thousands of bones in France suggest European Palaelodus lived in large flocks.
Australian and New Zealand Palaelodus species may have been less social due to few bones found across multiple localities.
Palaelodus belongs to the family Palaelodidae.
It is considered an important evolutionary link between flamingos and their closest relatives, the diving grebes, within the clade Mirandornithes.
The species Megapaloelodus goliath was originally classified as a type of Palaelodus but was later reclassified into the genus Megapaloelodus because of its more robust physical structure.
The extinct crane Pliogrus germanicus is now considered a type of palaelodid and may belong to the genus Palaelodus.
Palaelodus lived from the Rupelian to the Zanclean, between 33.9 and 5 million years ago.
The genus was most abundant during the Late Oligocene to Middle Miocene periods.
Isolated remains suggest that Palaelodus or a relative survived until the Pleistocene in Australia.
In Neogene Australia, Palaelodus species profited from salt lakes in the Lake Eyre Basin sharing habitat with derived flamingos like Phoenicopterus novaehollandiae.
Some researchers suggest Palaelodus was a diver using webbed feet for propulsion, but this hypothesis has been questioned by others who propose alternative lifestyles.
There is a debate over Palaelodus' lifestyle: Worthy et al. (2010) suggest they were wading birds similar to flamingos, while Mayr suggests a swimming lifestyle.
It is debated whether Palaelodus were divers or swam using stiff toes to feed on larvae and snails.
Some traits suggest Palaelodus kurochkini may represent a distinct genus rather than belonging to Palaelodus or Megapaloelodus.
Researchers debate whether Palaelodus gracilipes is a distinct species or just smaller individuals of the type species, noting that synonymizing them without further study might be premature.
